p: The Greek idiographos means written by the author himself, an autograph. The heading claims David wrote it personally.
b: Idiographos is a document in its writer's own hand. The heading gives the psalm "to David" (eis Dauid) and claims more for it than the other psalm titles do, one possible reason is to vouch for a psalm that stood apart from the rest, a guess and not a stated reason. Swete's notes show the word spelled oddly in one manuscript: the Verona Psalter (R) first has idiōtagraēphos, and a corrector changed it to idiographos. The Psalms Scroll from Qumran (11Q5), which has a Hebrew form of the psalm, heads it simply "Hallelujah. Of David son of Jesse."

p: The heading itself says the psalm is not one of the 150. The Orthodox Psalter opened for this page keeps that label.
b: The Greek says the psalm is "outside the number" (exōthen tou arithmou). The Greek manuscripts differ on the count: Swete's notes give the subscription of Codex Sinaiticus as "151 psalms of David" (the Greek numeral ona′), so Sinaiticus counts it in the total, while Codex Alexandrinus counts 150 psalms (rn′) and names the psalm "in his own hand" separately. An Orthodox Psalter in English (Asser, 2005) prints it after Psalm 150 with the note that it "is not numbered with the one hundred and fifty psalms," and an Orthodox parish's answer to a reader says it "has never been considered part of the body of the Psalms themselves." The Council of Trent defined "the Davidical Psalter, consisting of a hundred and fifty psalms." So the heading's own claim, that the psalm is David's but extra, is how the Orthodox Psalter and parish answer opened for this page treat it.

a: he fought Goliath man to man
p: The Greek verb means to fight in single combat, one champion against another, as Goliath demanded.
b: Monomacheō is to fight a duel. Goliath's challenge in 1 Samuel is exactly that: "Give me a man, and we will fight each other!" (1 Samuel 17:10). The heading ties the psalm to that day, though most of it is about David's youth and anointing (1 Samuel 16). The Greek title of Psalm 144 also names Goliath (see the note at Psalm 144:0), so the Greek Psalter remembers the battle twice. The name is spelled Goliad in Codex Vaticanus here, as in that title; Swete's notes give Goliath in Codex Alexandrinus.
orig: ὅτε ἐμονομάχησεν τῷ Γολιάδ (hote emonomachēsen tō Goliad)

a: Among my brothers I was small
p: The Hebrew of 11Q5 uses qatan, "small," the word 1 Samuel uses for David as the youngest son.
b: "The smallest one is left," Jesse tells Samuel, "but he's shepherding the flock" (1 Samuel 16:11), and again, "David was the smallest" (1 Samuel 17:14). Hebrew qatan means both little and youngest. The Hebrew psalm in 11Q5 begins, after its heading ("Hallelujah. Of David son of Jesse"), with that word: qaton hayiti min achai, "I was smaller than my brothers" (the transcription writes min above the line). The Greek has mikros, "small," and then neōteros, "younger," where the Hebrew has "younger than my father's sons."
orig: Μικρὸς ἤμην ... νεώτερος (mikros ēmēn ... neōteros); Hebrew קטן הייתי (qaton hayiti)

p: David the shepherd boy becomes Israel's shepherd. The New Testament takes up the picture for David's greater son.
b:
David tells Saul, "Your servant used to shepherd sheep for his father" (1 Samuel 17:34). Psalm 78 sums up the story: God "took him from the pens where the sheep were kept ... to be shepherd over Jacob, his people" (Psalm 78:70–71; compare 2 Samuel 7:8). The Hebrew psalm in 11Q5 says more: "he made me shepherd of his flock and ruler over his young goats," so the boy already rules a small kingdom.

A Christian reader can hear an echo in the shepherds of David's town at Jesus' birth (Luke 2:8–11) and in Jesus' "I am the good shepherd" (John 10:11). Psalm 151 itself does not look forward; the tie is in the Bible's larger picture of the shepherd king.

p: The Greek says only "an instrument." The Hebrew of 11Q5 names it: a pipe, paired with a lyre, as in Genesis 4:21.
b: Greek organon means a tool or a musical instrument in general. The Hebrew in 11Q5 reads yaday ʿasu ʿugav, weʾetsbeʿotay kinnor, "my hands made a pipe, and my fingers a lyre." The same two instruments, kinnor and ʿugav, are the first music in the Bible: Jubal "was the ancestor of everyone who plays the lyre and the pipe" (Genesis 4:21). Amos mocks those who "like David ... design musical instruments of their own" (Amos 6:5), and Chronicles speaks of "the instruments of David" (2 Chronicles 29:26). The psalm makes David not only a player but a maker.
orig: αἱ χεῖρές μου ἐποίησαν ὄργανον (hai cheires mou epoiēsan organon); Hebrew ידי עשו עוגב

p: The Greek verb means to fit together or tune. The Hebrew has kinnor, the lyre David played for Saul.
b: Psaltērion, from psallō, "pluck," is a stringed instrument, the word that gave English "psaltery" and, through the book of Psalms, "psalter." Harmozō means to join or fit, and of strings to tune. In 1 Samuel 16:16–23 David's instrument is the kinnor, the "lyre," and that is the word in 11Q5. The Plain English Translation renders the Greek as "harp" to keep the Greek and Hebrew words apart. Psalm 144, which the Greek titles "against Goliath," thanks God "who teaches my hands to fight a war, my fingers to do battle" (Psalm 144:1): there the same hands and fingers fight; here they make music.
orig: οἱ δάκτυλοί μου ἥρμοσαν ψαλτήριον (hoi daktyloi mou hērmosan psaltērion); Hebrew ואצבעותי כנור

p: The hardest line in the psalm. The Greek is short and unclear; the Hebrew has a longer and different thought.
b:
The Greek reads, word for word, "And who will announce to my lord? The Lord himself, he himself hears." It can mean: no one needs to tell God about the shepherd boy, because God hears for himself. "My lord" could also be a human master, Saul or Jesse, but the next line makes God the subject, so the Plain English Translation capitalizes "Lord." The manuscripts differ at the end of the line (see the variant), and Brenton printed it as "And who shall tell my Lord? the Lord himself, he himself hears."

The Hebrew in 11Q5 has something else: "For who can tell, who can speak, and who can recount the deeds of the Lord? Everything God saw, everything he heard, and he listened. The transcription ends the sentence after "the Lord" and marks one letter, the vav before "God," as uncertain; Tyler F. Williams's English of these lines divides them the same way (three-things.ca)." There, the question is who can praise God's works, and the answer is that God himself saw and heard the boy's praise. Sanders took the Greek as a shortened form of the Hebrew, which would explain its oddness.
orig: καὶ τίς ἀναγγελεῖ τῷ κυρίῳ μου; (kai tis anangelei tō kyriō mou)

t: An angel, or the prophet Samuel?
p: In 1 Samuel the LORD sends Samuel. The Greek says "his angel" (or "messenger"); the Hebrew of 11Q5 says "his prophet ... Samuel."
b: Greek angelos means "messenger" and, in the Bible, very often an angel. In 1 Samuel 16:1 God says to Samuel, "I will send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite," and Samuel anoints David (1 Samuel 16:13). The Hebrew in 11Q5 agrees with 1 Samuel: "He sent his prophet to anoint me, Samuel, to make me great." So the Greek angelos may be meant as the human messenger, Samuel, without naming him. Read as "angel," it goes beyond 1 Samuel, which has no angel in the story. The Plain English Translation keeps "angel," the usual sense of the word, and says here what the alternative is.
orig: ἐξαπέστειλεν τὸν ἄγγελον αὐτοῦ (exapesteilen ton angelon autou); Hebrew שלח נביאו

a: anointed me with the oil of his anointing
p: Samuel "anointed him there among his brothers." The Hebrew of 11Q5 says "holy oil," the words of Psalm 89:20.
b:
"Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him there among his brothers. And from that day on, the LORD's Spirit swept down on David" (1 Samuel 16:13). The Hebrew in 11Q5 says God "anointed me with holy oil and made me leader of his people and ruler over the children of his covenant," close to Psalm 89: "I have found David my servant and anointed him with my holy oil" (Psalm 89:20). Anointing marks David as the LORD's chosen king; in Greek chriō, "anoint," is the root of Christos, "Anointed One."

Some Greek manuscripts read "with the mercy of his anointing" (see the variant), a slip between two Greek words that sound alike.

a: My brothers were good-looking and big
p: The psalm puts 1 Samuel 16:6–10 in David's own mouth: the LORD passed over the handsome, tall brothers.
b: When Samuel saw Eliab he thought, "Surely the LORD's anointed stands here." But the LORD said, "Do not look at his face or how tall he stands ... the LORD sees the heart" (1 Samuel 16:6–7). Seven sons passed, and "The LORD has chosen none of these" (1 Samuel 16:10). The Hebrew in 11Q5 lingers on the brothers: "handsome in form and handsome in looks, tall in their stature, handsome with their hair," and then, "the LORD God did not choose them." The Greek is shorter. Both leave out that David too had "good looks" (1 Samuel 16:12); the psalm wants the contrast of the small boy and the big brothers.

p: The Greek verb eudokeō is the word the voice from heaven uses of Jesus at his baptism: "in you I take delight."
b: Eudokeō means to be pleased with, to choose with favor. The brothers did not please God; the youngest did. At Jesus' baptism the voice from heaven says, "You are my dearly loved Son; in you I take delight" (Luke 3:22; compare Matthew 3:17), the same verb. This is a link of words, not a quotation: the Greek psalm uses an ordinary Greek Bible word for God's choosing. The Hebrew in 11Q5 has "did not choose" (lo bachar), the word of 1 Samuel 16:8–10.
orig: οὐκ εὐδόκησεν ἐν αὐτοῖς Κύριος (ouk eudokēsen en autois Kyrios)

p: The Greek Bible calls the Philistines allophyloi, "people of another tribe." The site renders it "Philistine" in the histories.
b: Allophylos means "of another race," a foreigner, and the Greek translators of Samuel used it for the Philistines. The site renders it "the Philistine" where the Philistines are meant, as here. The Hebrew psalm in 11Q5 (the second poem, 151B) uses the name itself: "Then I saw a Philistine taunting from the ranks of the Philistines."

a: called down curses on me by his idols
p: 1 Samuel 17:43 says Goliath "called down curses on David by his gods." The Greek psalm calls them idols.
b: The Plain English Translation of 1 Samuel 17:43 reads, "Then the Philistine called down curses on David by his gods." The psalm says eidōla, "idols," the Greek Bible's scornful word for false gods. The story sets Goliath's gods against David's: Goliath cursed by his, and David answered, "I am coming at you in the name of the LORD of Armies" (1 Samuel 17:45).
orig: ἐπικατηράσατό με ἐν τοῖς εἰδώλοις αὐτοῦ (epikatērasato me en tois eidōlois autou)

p: David killed Goliath with a stone and cut off his head with Goliath's own sword (1 Samuel 17:49–51). The psalm keeps only the sword.
b: 1 Samuel stresses that "David had no sword in his hand" (1 Samuel 17:50): the stone struck the Philistine down, and then David "took hold of the man's sword, pulled it out of its sheath and finished him off, and he cut off his head with it" (1 Samuel 17:51). The psalm skips the sling and the stone and tells only the sword, "his own" (tēn par' autou machairan, literally "the sword from him"; para with the genitive means "from" or "belonging to," not a place at his side). Codex Alexandrinus has "that man's" (ekeinou) for "his," with the same sense (Swete's notes). The point is the same as David's own: "the LORD saves, and not by sword and spear" (1 Samuel 17:47); the enemy's own weapon ends him.

a: I lifted shame off the Israelites
p: David's first question at the battle was about the man who "lifts this shame off Israel" (1 Samuel 17:26). The psalm ends there.
b: "The man who strikes down this Philistine and lifts this shame off Israel, what will he get?" (1 Samuel 17:26). Greek oneidos is the disgrace of being taunted and not answering. Goliath had thrown "insults at the ranks of Israel" (1 Samuel 17:10); in the Hebrew of 11Q5 he is "taunting" (mecharef), the verb 1 Samuel uses for his insults. The psalm closes by giving David the answer to his own question.
orig: ἦρα ὄνειδος ἐξ υἱῶν Ἰσραήλ (ēra oneidos ex huiōn Israēl)
